This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite sum-free set - that is, there are no solutions to\[a=b_1+\cdots+b_r\]with $b_1<\cdots<b_r<a\in A$. How small can $a_{n+1}-a_n$ be? Is it possible that $a_{n+1}-a_n<n$?
#876: [Er75b][Er77c][Er98]
additive combinatorics
Erdős [Er98] writes that Graham 'recently proved' that there is such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}-a_n<n^{1+o(1)}$, and that Melfi proved a somewhat weaker result.
Erdős [Er62c] proved that a sum-free set has density zero. Deshouillers, Erdős, and Melfi [DEM99] constructed a sum-free set that grows like $a_n\sim n^{3+o(1)}$.
Luczak and Schoen [LuSc00] have proved that, for all large $N$,\[\lvert A\cap [1,N]\rvert\ll (N\log N)^{1/2},\]and that there exists a sum-free set $B$ such that\[\lvert B\cap [1,N]\rvert \gg \frac{N^{1/2}}{(\log N)^{1/2+o(1)}}\]for all large $N$.
In [Er75b] and [Er77c] Erdős asks to determine the maximum possible value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$. Erdős had proved this is $<100$, and Sullivan had shown that this is $<4$, and Sullivan conjectured the maximum is slightly larger than $2$.
See also [790].

 A log-free improvement follows from the results of Conlon--Fox--Pham: https://www.its.caltech.edu/~dconlon/subset_sums.pdf and Szemerédi--Vu: https://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v163-n1-p01.pdf.
Write $\Sigma(X)$ for the finite subset sums of $X$. Theorem 1.9 from the work of Conlon--Fox--Pham, inserted into the proof of Szemerédi--Vu, Corollary 1.4, gives an absolute $C$ such that, if $X(x)\ge C\sqrt{x}$ eventually, then $\{dm:m\ge M\}\subseteq\Sigma(X)$ for some $d,M\ge1$. Indeed, in Szemerédi--Vu's Lemma 6.4 the common differences are replaced successively by gcds, so the progressions remain homogeneous; their residue-correction and Graham-net argument then produces a tail of $d\mathbb N$.
Now suppose that $A$ satisfies the condition of the problem and $\liminf_{x\to\infty}A(x)/\sqrt{x}>C$. Choose an infinite $D=\{u_j\}\subset A$ with $u_j\ge j^4$, and put $X=A\setminus D$. Then $D(x)=O(x^{1/4})$, so $X(x)\ge C\sqrt{x}$ eventually. Hence $\{dm:m\ge M\}\subseteq\Sigma(X)$. By pigeonhole, there are $u<v$ in $D$ with $u\equiv v\pmod d$ and $v-u\ge Md$. Thus $v-u\in\Sigma(X)$, so $v=u+\sum_{s\in S}s$ for some nonempty finite $S\subset X$, a contradiction. Therefore $\liminf_{x\to\infty}A(x)/\sqrt{x}\le C$.

A partial proof 
claimed by Liam Price (using GPT 5.6 Sol Pro).
 Summary:
 GPT-5.6 Sol Pro proves that every infinite sum-free sequence \(A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) satisfies:\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{n}=\infty.
\]Consequently, \(a_{n+1}-a_n<n\) cannot hold for all sufficiently large \(n\), resolving the second question in the negative.
Interestingly, the proof uses Corollary 1.2 from Steve Fan's recent resolution of problem 254.
